Because the tenancy layer never constrains that `tenantId` to the only legitimate tenant (`default`) on a single-tenant deployment, an unauthenticated attacker simply supplies any unused tenant name to make the guard see an empty user list, and the endpoint then creates a brand-new CouchDB database (`<tenantId>_global-db`) and a **global-admin** user document (`admin.global = true`, `builder.global = true`) inside it - with no authentication and no CSRF token.

# Summary

With default flags, a pattern that contains several `*` wildcards takes polynomial time, O(n^k) for k stars, to reject a crafted file name. The pattern is an ordinary developer constant such as `*_*_*_*_*.csv`; only the string being matched comes from the attacker. A 255-byte file name (the maximum on common filesystems) takes 73 s with `fnmatch.fnmatch()` and 86 s with `glob.globmatch()`. The standard library's `fnmatch` handles the same input in under a millisecond.

This is different from GHSA-84v8-qmgq-9g88: that advisory covers extglob patterns, while this case needs no flags and no attacker-controlled pattern.

# Details

Every `*` is translated to a lazy `.*?` (`_STAR`, `wcmatch/_wcparse.py:212`; `_PATH_STAR` `[^/]*?`, `:218`), which is emitted in `_handle_star` (`:1405-1424`):

```text
*_*_*_*_*.csv  ->  ^(?s:(?=.)(?![.]).*?_.*?_.*?_.*?_.*?\.csv)$
```

When the subject consists of many `_` and does not end in `.csv`, the regex engine tries every way of splitting it between the stars. CPython fixed the same problem in its own `fnmatch` (bpo-40480) by making every star segment except the last one atomic.

# PoC

```python
import time, fnmatch as std
from wcmatch import fnmatch, glob

for pat, n in [('*_*_*_*.csv', 255), ('*_*_*_*.csv', 400), ('*_*_*_*_*.csv', 150),
               ('*_*_*_*_*.csv', 200), ('*_*_*_*_*.csv', 255)]:
    name = '_' * n
    t = time.perf_counter(); fnmatch.fnmatch(name, pat); w = time.perf_counter() - t
    t = time.perf_counter(); std.fnmatchcase(name, pat); s = time.perf_counter() - t
    print(f'{pat:15} len={n}  wcmatch={w:.3f}s  stdlib={s:.5f}s')

t = time.perf_counter(); glob.globmatch('uploads/' + '_' * 255, 'uploads/*_*_*_*_*.csv')
print(f'globmatch {time.perf_counter() - t:.2f}s')
```

wcmatch 11.1, CPython 3.13, macOS:

```text
*_*_*_*.csv     len=255  wcmatch=1.412s   stdlib=0.00001s
*_*_*_*.csv     len=400  wcmatch=8.599s   stdlib=0.00004s
*_*_*_*_*.csv   len=150  wcmatch=5.333s   stdlib=0.00003s
*_*_*_*_*.csv   len=200  wcmatch=22.415s  stdlib=0.00007s
*_*_*_*_*.csv   len=255  wcmatch=72.732s  stdlib=0.00047s
globmatch 85.75s
```

`glob.glob('*_*_*_*.csv', root_dir=d)` on a real directory that contains one file named `'_' * 255` takes 1.7 s.

# Impact

Applications that match untrusted names against multi-star patterns can be blocked on a single CPU core for minutes per name. Examples: upload handlers, archive or object-store key filters, and `glob`/`WcMatch` scans of directories where other users can create files. No authentication is needed.

# Fix

Emit every star segment except the last one as an atomic group, as the standard library does. On Python 3.11 and later use `(?>.*?_)`; on 3.10 use the lookahead/backreference form from `fnmatch._join_translated_parts`. For example:

```text
^(?s:(?=.)(?![.])(?>.*?_)(?>.*?_)(?>.*?_)(?>.*?_).*?\.csv)$
```

This rejects the 255-byte name in under 1 ms. On my spot-check inputs it gives the same results as the current regex. The same change applies to `_PATH_STAR`.

Commit `23e8cca3136a` hardened the search-result title against insert-tag/XSS by setting `$objTemplate->title = StringUtil::specialchars(StringUtil::stripInsertTags($arrResult[$i]['title']))`. But the legacy HTML5 template does not use that `title` variable - it prints the raw `link` variable, which is assigned without escaping.

## Impact

Affected configuration (important): on 5.7.9 the default search template is the Twig `search_default.html.twig`, which does not use the raw `link` variable and auto-escapes - so a default Twig install is not affected. The vulnerable raw echo is in the legacy `search_default.html5` template (still shipped and selectable in 5.7.9, line 8: `<?= $this->link ?>`); exploitation requires that legacy template to be active for the search module (common on sites migrated from earlier Contao / using custom template selection). Where the legacy template is used, the sink is unambiguously raw and `ModuleSearch::compile()` assigns `link` from the entity-decoded indexed title.

A backend page editor can store script that executes for anonymous front-end visitors (and admins) viewing search results, a stored XSS crossing the editor -> anonymous-visitor boundary.

## Credits

This security vulnerability was found by @HDWSec

Commit `2b83a60f7763` (5.7.3) hardened the template editor: it added `TemplateEditorModuleVoter` + `CheckTemplateEditorSaveListener` so a non-admin cannot self-grant the `tpl_editor` backend module (editable PHP-capable templates permit server-side code execution). That voter supports only the `modules` field and the literal value `tpl_editor`.

The equally RCE-capable `theme_import` capability lives in a different field - the `themes` checkbox field (tl_user_group.php:98-105 options include `theme_import`; identical on tl_user.php:248-253) - which has no save_callback and no voter. `TemplateEditorModuleVoter` is the only DC voter registered for tl_user_group, and it does not cover the `themes` field. So a delegated user manager can add `theme_import` to their own (or a managed) account.

Live repro (Contao 5.7.9):
1. As admin, create a non-admin backend group with the `user` (or `group`) module (a delegated user manager), and a user in it. Confirm the user cannot access `tpl_editor` (blocked by the 5.7.3 voter).
2. As that non-admin, edit a group/account: add `themes` to the modules field and `theme_import` to the themes field (both accepted - only `tpl_editor` is blocked). Re-authenticate.

## Impact

A delegated user/group manager (a role explicitly not trusted with template/code access) escalates to arbitrary PHP execution on the server, fully compromising the installation. This bypasses the exact protection the 5.7.3 `tpl_editor` fix introduced.

## Credits

This security vulnerability was found by @HDWSec

Channel access is enforced only by the DataContainer voters (`NewsletterChannelAccessVoter` / `NewsletterRecipientsAccessVoter`, requiring USER_CAN_EDIT_CHANNEL), whose `supportsType()` fires exclusively for Create/Read/Update/DeleteAction subjects dispatched inside DC_Table's create/edit/delete methods. ## Impact

A channel-scoped newsletter editor can inject recipients into, mass-mail, and in some versions, delete/denylist recipients of channels they are not authorized to edit - defeating the per-channel permission model (integrity + abuse of the mail-sending capability).

### Summary

Extracting an attacker-supplied 7z archive can write files outside the destination directory. The 7z header stores each entry's path as a UTF-16 name with nothing constraining it to a relative, in-tree path. The extractor joins that name onto the destination and writes to the result without normalizing it or checking that it stays under the destination root, so an entry named `../../etc/cron.d/x` or an absolute path escapes the target.

### Details

In `src/util/decompress.rs`, `decompress_impl` computes the per-entry destination directly (line 140):

```rust
let dest_path = dest.join(entry.name());
extract_fn(entry, reader, &dest_path)
```

`default_entry_extract_fn` (line 154) then acts on that path:

```rust
let file = File::create(path)
    .map_err(|e| Error::file_open(e, path.to_string_lossy().to_string()))?;
```

There is no normalization, no `dest_path.starts_with(dest)` check, and no symlink-entry handling. `Path::join` discards the base when the joined component is absolute, and `..` components are not collapsed against the base. The convenience entry points (`decompress`, `decompress_file`, `decompress_with_password`, `decompress_file_with_password`) all route through `decompress_impl` with `default_entry_extract_fn`, so the default API is affected.

The trust boundary is the archive bytes. Any caller that extracts an untrusted `.7z` reaches the sink.

### PoC

1. Build a `.7z` whose `FilesInfo` contains an entry named `../../../../tmp/pwned` (or, on Windows, an absolute path such as `C:\Windows\Temp\pwned`).
2. Call `sevenz_rust2::decompress_file("evil.7z", "./out")`.
3. The file is created at the traversed location outside `./out`. Targeting a startup/cron path or a config file turns the write into code execution or persistence.

### Impact

Arbitrary file write outside the intended directory (CWE-22 / CWE-23, the Zip-Slip class). On extraction of an attacker-controlled archive, an entry overwrites files outside the destination — config, cron, autostart, or build artifacts — which can escalate to code execution. Reachable by upload-handling backends, malware-analysis sandboxes, mod/game installers, and CI steps that unpack user-supplied 7z files.

### Suggested remediation

Reject any entry whose name contains a `ParentDir`, `RootDir`, or `Prefix` component, or canonicalize the joined path and verify `starts_with(dest)` before creating it. Apply the guard inside `default_entry_extract_fn` (and `decompress_impl`) so the hardening is the default rather than left to each caller. Reject or explicitly opt-in symlink entries.

## Maintainer response

This issue was patched with ef760b61f3535ac8b93006212aef41bfebc237eb and released as `v0.21.1` to crates.io

Consumers that extract attacker-supplied archives received over a network without user interaction should re-score as AV:N/UI:N (≈8.6).

### Summary
A remote Denial of Service (DoS) vulnerability, allows any remote client to cause a complete crash of the Aedes MQTT broker process. This is achieved by sending a specially crafted MQTT message (via PUBLISH or SUBSCRIBE), or by setting a Will message with such a topic, containing a highly recursive topic string (e.g., with thousands of '/' delimiters). The lack of input validation and error handling leads to an uncaught exception in an internal routing library, terminating the entire Node.js application.

### Details
The Aedes broker fails to enforce limits on the depth or structural complexity of MQTT topic strings. When a client publishes to or subscribes to a topic with excessive levels of recursion, the internal routing logic cascading into the qlobber library (via mqemitter) reaches an hard-coded limit within the qlobber._split_words function.

This function throws a hard Error: too many words (found in lib/qlobber.js:604). Crucially, Aedes does not wrap the calls to these internal modules (such as in handlers/subscribe.js or the publishing logic) in try-catch blocks. ### Background

NATS.io is a high performance open source pub-sub distributed communication technology, built for the cloud, on-premise, IoT and edge computing.

The NATS Server supports leafnode connections between servers and message tracing through NATS headers.

### Problem Description

Message trace destination checks were applied to ordinary client connections but not consistently to messages arriving through leafnode connections.

A leafnode operator could cause trace events to be sent to subjects that would not otherwise be permitted and could use trace-only behavior to prevent normal delivery or storage of affected messages.

Trace events can include routing, subscription, account, service import and JetStream metadata. The payload of the original application message is not chosen through the trace event itself.

### Affected Versions

Versions v2.14.2, v2.12.7 and below are vulnerable. The issue is fixed in v2.14.3 and v2.12.8.

### Workarounds

Where possible, avoid granting publish paths from less-trusted leaf nodes into subjects for which trace-only behavior would affect delivery guarantees. No other known workarounds are available aside from upgrading to a fixed release.

### References

 * GHSA advisory: <https://github.com/nats-io/nats-server/security/advisories/GHSA-p3j5-5hrq-p75h>
 * Credit: Koda Reef

`chcon` resolved recursive targets from `fts_accpath` with a fresh path lookup, so traversal and the SELinux get/set were not bound to traversal directory state. A privileged recursive relabel can be redirected to unintended objects under rename/symlink races. Fix opens targets with `openat` against the traversal cwd fd before the SELinux operation.

## Summary:

OHttpClientCodec and OHttpServerCodec retain the encrypted outer HttpContent in a handler-level cumulationBuffer. After a valid OHTTP exchange completes, the OHTTP request/response context is destroyed, but the outer cumulationBuffer is not released or reset. It remains referenced by the codec until a later inbound content frame replaces it or the handler is removed/channel is closed.

This can pin attacker-influenced pooled/direct buffer capacity on idle keep-alive channels. Across many long-lived idle connections, this can create availability pressure.

Affected components:

* codec-ohttp/src/main/java/io/netty/incubator/codec/ohttp/OHttpClientCodec.java
* codec-ohttp/src/main/java/io/netty/incubator/codec/ohttp/OHttpServerCodec.java
* codec-ohttp/src/main/java/io/netty/incubator/codec/ohttp/OHttpRequestResponseContext.java

## Root cause:

OHttpClientCodec retains inbound content into a handler-level cumulationBuffer. On LastHttpContent, it destroys only the OHttpRequestResponseContextHolder. The cumulationBuffer is released in handlerRemoved(), not immediately after successful exchange completion.

OHttpServerCodec follows the same pattern: it retains inbound content into a handler-level cumulationBuffer, and on completed request/response it destroys the OHttpRequestResponseContext. The outer cumulationBuffer remains owned by the codec and is released only when the handler is removed.

OHttpRequestResponseContext.parse() consumes bytes from the caller-provided outer cumulation buffer, but its destroy() path releases only the inner binary HTTP cumulation, not the codec-level outer cumulationBuffer.

## PoC:

A local test only:

```
codec-ohttp/src/test/java/io/netty/incubator/codec/ohttp/OHttpCumulationBufferRetentionTest.java
```

The test reuses existing OHTTP test helpers and BouncyCastle crypto provider to perform valid completed OHTTP exchanges over EmbeddedChannel pairs. It sends both a small and a large request/response exchange, confirms completion, then reflects the private cumulationBuffer field from both OHttpClientCodec and OHttpServerCodec.

Command:

```
./mvnw -pl codec-ohttp -Dtest=OHttpCumulationBufferRetentionTest -DfailIfNoTests=false test
```

Observed output:

```
small client after completion: refCnt=1 capacity=1064 readerIndex=1064 writerIndex=1064 readableBytes=0
small server after completion: refCnt=1 capacity=1110 readerIndex=1110 writerIndex=1110 readableBytes=0
large client after completion: refCnt=1 capacity=262144 readerIndex=131114 writerIndex=131114 readableBytes=0
large server after completion: refCnt=1 capacity=262144 readerIndex=131160 writerIndex=131160 readableBytes=0
small after close: clientOldRefCnt=0 serverOldRefCnt=0
large after close: clientOldRefCnt=0 serverOldRefCnt=0
Tests run: 1, Failures: 0, Errors: 0, Skipped: 0
BUILD SUCCESS
```

Interpretation:

After completion, both the client and server cumulationBuffer objects have:

* refCnt=1
* readableBytes=0
* large retained capacity for the large exchange
* channel still open/active
* OHTTP context completed/destroyed

After channel close/handler removal, the previously retained buffers are released and their old refCnt values become 0.

## Impact:

A peer can complete a large valid OHTTP request/response and keep the connection open. The codec retains the high-water outer cumulation buffer for the lifetime of the idle keep-alive channel, or until a later inbound content frame replaces it. Across many idle keep-alive channels, this can pin pooled/direct memory and create availability pressure.

This is not unbounded growth per exchange on a single channel. The more precise impact is connection-lifetime retention of the current consumed high-water outer cumulation buffer.

## Suggested fix:

After successful LastHttpContent processing, release and reset the codec-level outer cumulationBuffer once parsing has consumed the complete message and no unread bytes remain.

Care is needed not to release the buffer if unread byt

### Impact

When fetching objects from a malicious repository, Git LFS may execute an arbitrary command or binary after failing to sufficiently restrict the set of configuration options defined in an `.lfsconfig` file in the repository.

Git LFS permits a limited set of configuration options to be defined in an `.lfsconfig` file at the root of a Git repository, but does not filter these options correctly if their keys contain certain additional components, which allows an attacker to mimic options that configure Git LFS to use a custom command to transfer objects.  An attacker can then provide an arbitrary command which Git LFS will invoke when fetching objects.

Git LFS has resolved this issue by correctly restricting the configuration of custom object transfer commands to local Git configuration files.

### Patches

This problem exists in all versions since 1.3.0 and is patched in v3.8.1. All users should upgrade to v3.8.1.

### Workarounds

No single workaround exists other than to disable Git LFS entirely. As far as possible, users and administrators should avoid cloning repositories from untrusted sources.

### For more information

If you have any questions or comments about this advisory:
* For general questions, start a discussion in the Git LFS [discussion forum](https://github.com/git-lfs/git-lfs/discussions).
* For reports of additional vulnerabilities, please follow the Git LFS [security reporting policy](https://github.com/git-lfs/git-lfs/blob/main/SECURITY.md).

### Impact

When fetching objects from a malicious repository, Git LFS may execute an arbitrary command or binary after incorrectly parsing the Git configuration options defined for a submodule.

Git LFS reads Git configuration options without checking for embedded line-ending control characters.  By inserting control characters such as line feed (LF) into certain values, an attacker may be able to mimic options that cause Git LFS to execute an arbitrary command when fetching or adding objects.

Git LFS has resolved this issue by always using an unambiguous format to read and parse Git configuration options.

### Patches

This problem exists in all versions since 0.6.0 and is patched in v3.8.1. All users should upgrade to v3.8.1.

### Workarounds

To work around the problem, users should prevent Git from initializing any submodules by disabling the `fetch.recurseSubmodules` and `submodule.recurse` configuration options and by never running the `git submodule init` command.  Any submodules which have already been initialized in a repository may be deactivated with the `git submodule deinit` command.

### For more information

If you have any questions or comments about this advisory:
* For general questions, start a discussion in the Git LFS [discussion forum](https://github.com/git-lfs/git-lfs/discussions).

### Summary
storyblok-backup writes files using unsanitized names for Storyblok components, which are content type or schema definitions. This allows a component name containing path traversal sequences to cause backup files to be written outside the intended backup directory. Anyone with component management access in the source Storyblok space, not server access, can plant a malicious component name that causes arbitrary file writes on the machine of anyone who later runs a backup against that space.

### Details
The writeJson function, which takes a folder, a file name, and content, builds the output file path by directly concatenating the backup directory, the folder, and the file name as strings, with no path sanitization or containment check.

For the components resource type specifically, the file name used is the component's own name field, which is free text and editable by anyone with component management access in the Storyblok CMS.

Other resource types are not affected by this same issue. Stories and datasources use their numeric IDs as filenames, and assets have their filename derived by splitting on the slash character and taking the last segment, which strips path separators. This issue is scoped specifically to components.

Since the component name is stored in Storyblok and only read back later when the backup tool runs, this is a stored, second order vulnerability. The malicious value is planted once, then triggers on every subsequent backup run performed by anyone using this tool against that Storyblok space.

### PoC

**Step 1 — plant the malicious component name via Storyblok's Management API:**

curl -X POST "https://mapi.storyblok.com/v1/spaces/<SPACE_ID>/components/" \
  -H "Authorization: <MANAGEMENT_API_TOKEN>" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "component": {
      "name": "../../../../tmp/evil-storyblok-backup",
      "schema": {}
    }
  }'

Any Storyblok user with component-management permission in the space (not server access to wherever backups run) can do this through the Storyblok UI just as easily, by naming a new component with this value in the component name field.

**Step 2 — run storyblok-backup against this space, exactly as a normal user would:**

npx storyblok-backup \
  --space <SPACE_ID> \
  --token <MANAGEMENT_API_TOKEN> \
  --path ./backup \
  --types "components"

**Step 3 — observe the actual file write location:**

With the malicious component name above, the tool's writeJson() function builds the output path as:

  backupDir + "/components" + "/../../../../tmp/evil-storyblok-backup" + ".json"

which resolves outside ./backup entirely. Confirm with:

  ls -la /tmp/evil-storyblok-backup.json

The file exists there, outside the --path ./backup directory that was configured, containing the full JSON definition of the malicious component.

**Step 4 — for comparison, confirm assets and stories are NOT affected:**

The same defaultFetch() pattern is used for stories and datasources (fileField: numeric id) and for assets (fileField derived via 
.split('/').at(-1), which strips any path separators from the value before it reaches writeJson()). Only the components resource type passes a raw, unsanitized user-editable string directly into the file path.

### Impact
Anyone with the ability to create or rename a component in the source Storyblok space, which is a content management privilege and not server access, can cause the backup tool, when run by someone else, to write files outside the intended backup directory on whatever machine runs the backup. Depending on the path chosen and the permissions of the process running the backup, this could overwrite existing files at attacker chosen locations on the host filesystem.

Suggested fix: sanitize the component name before using it as a filename, for example by applying the same last-path-segment treatment already used for assets, or by resolving the final path and verifying it stays within the intended backup director

### Impact

`amqtt` is vulnerable to a remote denial of service caused by incomplete MQTT QoS 2 transactions remaining allocated after the associated client disconnects.

MQTT QoS 2 uses a four-step handshake to provide exactly-once delivery. If a client begins a QoS 2 transaction but disconnects before the handshake completes, `amqtt` retains the associated transaction state and packet identifier without an expiration mechanism to remove it.

QoS 1 transactions are protected by a timeout mechanism, which defaults to 5 seconds, allowing abandoned state to be released. Equivalent timeout handling was not applied to incomplete QoS 2 transactions.

An attacker can repeatedly connect to the broker, initiate QoS 2 transactions, and disconnect before completing the handshake. Each incomplete transaction leaves state allocated in memory. Repeating this process causes broker memory consumption to grow continuously.

Successful exploitation can cause:

* Unbounded growth in broker memory usage
* Accumulation of incomplete QoS 2 transaction state
* Increasing memory pressure on the host system
* Termination of the broker process when available memory is exhausted
* Operating-system Out-Of-Memory (OOM) intervention
* Complete loss of availability for the affected broker process

Exploitation does not require maintaining long-lived connections. An attacker can create incomplete QoS 2 transactions and disconnect, leaving the broker to retain the associated state after the network connection has closed.

Under the default configuration, anonymous clients can exploit the vulnerability without credentials. When authentication is enabled, any authenticated client permitted to initiate QoS 2 message flows may still be able to exploit it. Authentication alone is therefore not a sufficient mitigation.

* Ecosystem: `pip`
* Package: `amqtt`
* Affected versions: `>= 0.11.0, <= 0.12.0`

The vulnerable code is present in the v0.11.0 release commit, 352678c87e50e501a8a5bb91fab73c9400fa046c, and remained present on the main branch as of 5ebbf366f6b79ab12a06f426ffd18ff28954e4ea. Versions before 0.11.0 were not evaluated.

This is a denial-of-service vulnerability only. No confidentiality or integrity impact has been identified. Successful exploitation causes degradation and eventual loss of availability through memory exhaustion.

### Patches

The issue will be been patched in the `v0.12.1` released version; all users should upgrade.

The completed fix:

* Apply transaction expiration handling consistently to incomplete QoS 1 and QoS 2 message flows
* Expire abandoned QoS 2 state when the associated transaction does not complete within the configured timeout
* Release the associated message state and packet identifiers when the transaction expires
* Prevent disconnected clients from leaving incomplete QoS 2 transactions resident in broker memory indefinitely

The fixing commit is [`2755fd801a6f95e9b73e11116948b57a95348466`](https://github.com/Yakifo/amqtt/commit/2755fd801a6f95e9b73e11116948b57a95348466)

### Workarounds

Administrators who cannot immediately upgrade should limit the ability of untrusted clients to create large numbers of incomplete QoS 2 transactions.

Where application requirements permit, preventing untrusted clients from using QoS 2 provides the strongest temporary mitigation.

Connection and request rate limiting at a reverse proxy, load balancer, firewall, or other network layer can reduce the rate at which an attacker creates abandoned transactions, but does not eliminate the underlying vulnerability. An attacker able to continue creating incomplete QoS 2 transactions can still cause memory usage to increase over time.

Administrators should also monitor broker memory consumption and configure appropriate process or container memory limits to prevent exhaustion of host resources. Restarting the broker may reclaim abandoned state and restore availability, but the broker remains vulnerable until the patched version is installed.

### Summary

The email second factor is an mt_rand() six-digit code verified with no attempt limit or lockout

The email second factor is a six-digit code drawn from `mt_rand()` and verified with no attempt limit, so an attacker who already has the password can brute-force it inside its validity window.

`lib/Domain/Service/MfaService.php`, in `generateEmailVerificationCode()`:

```php
$numericCode = mt_rand(100000, 999999);
```

That is a 900,000-value space, and `mt_rand()` is a Mersenne Twister rather than a CSPRNG, so it is not appropriate for a security token in the first place. PHP provides `random_int()` for exactly this.

The bigger problem is that nothing limits guesses. `lib/Application/Controller/MfaVerifyController.php` calls:

```php
$isValid = $this->mfaService->verifyCode($userId, $code);
```

and on failure the only action taken is:

```php
$this->logger->warning('[MfaVerifyController] Verification failed for user ID: {user_id}', ['user_id' => $userId]);
```

I grepped that controller for any counter, lockout, throttle or rate limit and found nothing beyond log statements. So an attacker holding valid credentials submits codes until one lands. Against 900,000 values with no ceiling on attempts, the only thing standing in the way is the code's validity window and however fast requests can be issued.

That defeats the purpose of the second factor: it is meant to hold even when the password is known, and here it reduces to a race the attacker is likely to win with sustained requests.

Two separate fixes, and I would treat the second as the urgent one:

1. Generate the code with `random_int(100000, 999999)` so it is not predictable from RNG state.
2. Enforce a failed-attempt counter tied to the user and the pending MFA session, invalidating the code and requiring a fresh one after a small number of wrong guesses, plus a per-account and per-IP rate limit on the verify endpoint.

Scope: source-verified at `master`. I confirmed the generator, the verify call site, the log-only failure handling and the absence of any throttling construct in that controller. I did not stand up a Poweradmin instance and run a brute-force against a live code, so the rate at which the space can be covered in practice is not something I measured. If throttling is applied at a layer I did not look at, such as a web-server or reverse-proxy rule shipped with your deployment docs, then the second half of this weakens considerably and I would want to know that.

I used AI assistance while reading the code and preparing this report.

---

Confirmed, and thanks for the detail. I've widened the affected range: this reaches back to 4.0.0, where MFA was first added, and 4.4.0 still ships it, so the original <= 4.3.4 was too narrow. The 3.x line has no MFA at all and is unaffected. Fixes are in for 4.2.x, 4.3.x, 4.4.x and the development branch.

To answer your question about other layers, there is nothing. No middleware runs in front of that controller, so what you found missing in the controller is the whole picture.

I've adjusted the score down from 9.1 to 7.4. Walking 900,000 values inside the code's ten minute life needs sustained request rates, and MFA is off by default, so there are real preconditions beyond knowing the password. It is still a second factor that does not hold, which is the point of the report.

The mt_rand swap is in as well, though I would treat that as hardening rather than the bug. Recovering the generator state from these codes is not practical in this setup. The missing attempt limit was the actual problem.

## Summary

Route selection uses the raw un-normalized request path, and the per-route ACL and basic-auth gates hang off that selection, so a dot-segment, encoded-dot, or double-slash variant of a protected path selects a different route, skips both gates, and is forwarded to the backend which normalizes and serves the protected resource. Unauthenticated; complete bypass of the access control the operator configured. Confirmed at HEAD b841544. Direct peers: Traefik CVE-2023-47106, Envoy CVE-2019-9901.

## The defect

fabio never normalizes the request path. A repository-wide search for path.Clean returns zero results. Route selection uses the raw path (route/table.go line 487: `if target = t.lookup(h, req.URL.Path, pick, match); target != nil {`). Both access-control gates are properties of the target that lookup returned:

```go
// proxy/http_proxy.go
if t.AccessDeniedHTTP(r) {                      // line 111, per-route allow / deny:ip ACL
    http.Error(w, "access denied", http.StatusForbidden)
    return
}
if !t.Authorized(r, w, p.AuthSchemes) {          // line 116, per-route auth= basic auth
    http.Error(w, "authorization failed", http.StatusUnauthorized)
    return
}
```

and the same raw path is forwarded verbatim (`Path: r.URL.Path` at line 142). So /./admin/, /%2e/admin/, //admin/ and /x/../admin/ do not match the protected /admin route. They fall through to the catch-all / route, which carries no ACL and no auth, and fabio forwards the un-normalized path to the origin, which normalizes it and serves the protected resource.

## Verification

Verified end to end against the real binary at HEAD, not a synthetic unit test. fabio was built and run with static routes against a `python3 -m http.server` origin, driven with curl --path-as-is: on a basic-auth route, /admin/ returned 401 without credentials and 200 with valid credentials (controls correct), while all four crafted paths returned 200 with the protected page and NO credentials; on an ACL route, /admin/ returned 403 and all four crafted variants returned 200.

Precondition, stated honestly: a less restrictive route must reach the same backend so the crafted path has somewhere to fall through to. That is exactly the two-tag urlprefix- shape fabio's own access-control documentation instructs operators to configure. Where no fallback route exists the request 404s instead.

## Suggested fix

Normalize the path before route lookup: decode percent-encoded dot segments and apply path.Clean, then match. Whether the normalized or original path is forwarded upstream is a separate decision, but the LOOKUP must run on the normalized form, because the ACL and auth decisions are derived from it. Also lowercase and strip the port and any trailing dot from the request host before host matching. Secondary observations: X-Forwarded-Prefix is passed through from the client on non-strip routes; the gRPC proxy path never calls either authorization gate, so allow=/auth= on a proto=grpc route are silently unenforced.

## Dedup note

The obvious residual of CVE-2025-48865 is already taken: CVE-2026-62987 / GHSA-fq95-v8xc-jm3v (published 2026-07-03) covers the Connection-header strip of proxy.header.clientip/tls/requestid, fixed in v1.7.2. Do not re-report that. The finding above is a different and independent defect.

## Tooling

AI assistance was used while investigating. The bypass was reproduced against the real fabio binary with a live backend, including the 401-vs-200 and 403-vs-200 controls, and the reporter separately confirmed at HEAD that lookup takes req.URL.Path, that both gates derive from the returned target, that the raw path is forwarded, and that path.Clean appears nowhere in the repository.

The reporter manually verified this finding against the project's source at the location cited above before reporting it; the AI assistance noted above was for the audit and the drafting.

### Impact

After receiving an HTTP redirection, Git LFS may forward certain HTTP headers to a host other than the one for which they were intended.  While `Authorization` headers are never forwarded to inappropriate hosts, `Cookie` headers may be forwarded incorrectly.

Git LFS has resolved this issue by never forwarding `Cookie` headers to hosts other than the ones for which they were intended.  In particular, after an HTTP redirection is received to a URL with a different scheme, host, or port than found in the URL of the current request, any `Authorization` and `Cookie` headers from the current request will not be sent in the redirected request.

### Patches

This problem exists in all versions since 0.5.0 and is patched in v3.8.1. All users should upgrade to v3.8.1.

### Workarounds

No single workaround exists.  As far as possible, users and administrators should review their systems to confirm no unnecessary HTTP redirections are performed, and that HTTP headers other than `Authorization` do not contain privileged or confidential information.

### For more information

If you have any questions or comments about this advisory:
* For general questions, start a discussion in the Git LFS [discussion forum](https://github.com/git-lfs/git-lfs/discussions).
* For reports of additional vulnerabilities, please follow the Git LFS [security reporting policy](https://github.com/git-lfs/git-lfs/blob/main/SECURITY.md).

### Impact

When Git LFS makes object transfer or authentication requests to a remote host via SSH, it passes the path component of the remote's SSH URL as part of a command to be executed, but does not properly format the URL's path component as a single argument.  By inserting shell meta-characters into the SSH URL, an attacker may be able to execute arbitrary commands on the remote host, if the host passes the commands to a shell without sanitizing them first.

Git LFS has resolved this problem by fully quoting the arguments of the remote commands it sends via SSH.

As well, Git LFS has resolved a problem with the default HTTPS URLs used when an SSH URL is configured for a remote host and the host either does not support Git LFS remote commands sent via SSH or supports HTTP authentication via SSH for Git LFS but does not return an explicit HTTP URL in response to a `git-lfs-authenticate` remote command.  In these cases, Git LFS now correctly encodes the HTTPS URL used to contact the remote host.

### Patches

This problem exists in all versions since 0.5.0 and is patched in v3.8.1. All users should upgrade to v3.8.1.

### Workarounds

Users may set the `lfs.sshTransfer` Git configuration option to `never`, after which Git LFS will not attempt any object transfers over SSH.  However, Git LFS will still make authentication requests to SSH URLs, so administrators of Git LFS services should ensure their systems sanitize all commands received over SSH before executing them.
